import cmath
# Eq. (9), taking z_p to mean the defined vertex v_p.
a=[0.4, 1.3, 2.7]

strengths: The paper addresses an important microscopy problem through an interpretable inverse-rendering framework that jointly represents surface geometry and microscope blur, without requiring labeled training data.

Representing fluorescent membranes as surface distributions and convolving them with a PSF in Fourier space is a principled approach. The custom CUDA implementation and spectral truncation address practical computational obstacles; Figure 6 demonstrates substantial acceleration over vectorized implementations.

The four synthetic reconstructions and the 4-, 6-, and 16-cell embryo examples provide encouraging feasibility evidence, including reconstruction with non-manifold meshes representing shared cell interfaces.

The pipeline figures communicate the approach clearly. The manuscript cites its biological data and inherited methods, provides an implementation link, and appropriately acknowledges remaining computational limitations.
weaknesses: Reconstruction accuracy is insufficiently established. Figures 7–8 primarily show visual examples and image-loss curves, without quantitative surface errors, segmentation metrics, or comparisons with relevant active-mesh or deconvolution methods. Even the synthetic experiments omit geometric evaluation despite having ground-truth meshes. The examples support feasibility but do not adequately substantiate accurate recovery of fine geometry.

The central claim of recovering both geometry and PSF lacks controlled validation. Section 5.2 generates images with the proposed renderer and supplies the true PSF during reconstruction. The real examples provide no independent PSF reference or geometric ground truth. Consequently, low image residuals cannot establish that fitted blur represents the optics rather than compensating for geometry or intensity mismatch. Initialization sensitivity and robustness to noise or nonuniform fluorescence are also untested.

Several equations require correction before the numerical method can be reproduced confidently. Under the Fourier convention in Eq. (6), Eq. (4) should contain Sigma rather than its inverse. The vertex-projection denominators in Eq. (11) also do not match differentiation of the edge-based expression in Eq. (9). These may be transcription errors, but the manuscript supplies no numerical gradient checks or accuracy tests around the singular cases addressed in Section 4.2.3.

The evidence for spectral acceleration is weaker than the accompanying claim: Table 1 demonstrates approximately 2× forward and 2.9× backward speedups, whereas Section 5.1.1 cites it for potential orders-of-magnitude savings. The table still reports roughly 18.8 seconds per mesh forward/backward pair. End-to-end reconstruction times and measurements of accuracy versus frequency cutoff are needed to assess the practical benefit.

The contribution beyond the cited Fourier-transform methods [27,38], deconvolving active contours [23,54], and optimization method [55] needs sharper delineation. Ablations do not isolate the benefits of learned PSF parameters, spectral truncation, or the optimizer. Although the loss avoids explicit shape penalties, Eq. (17) applies Laplacian gradient smoothing with lambda = 50; this should be distinguished clearly from eliminating smoothing priors.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the implementation link: learning rates, the precise alternation schedule, PSF initialization and positive-definite covariance parameterization, intensity preprocessing, and the numerical switching threshold are not adequately specified.
